blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears **at least twice**, and `false` if every value is distinct.

blocks.alt: 1, 2, 3, 1 sorted becomes 1, 1, 2, 3. The two 1s, far apart before, are now neighbours, so comparing each value with the one before it finds the duplicate.

blocks.text: The pattern: sort first, then scan

Many questions are hard on a jumbled array and easy on a sorted one. **Sorting puts related values next to each other**: equal values become neighbours, the closest pair of numbers sits side by side, and intervals line up by start time so overlaps are adjacent. After an O(n log n) sort, a single O(n) scan comparing neighbours (or tracking a running value) finishes the job.

The cost to remember: sorting is O(n log n) and either modifies the input or needs a copy. When a hash map can answer the question in O(n), it's faster — but sorting needs no extra memory if you may reorder the input, and it's the only easy route when the question is about **order** (closest, overlapping, the h-th largest). The questions in this chapter all follow this shape.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** About n²/2 comparisons — too slow for 10⁵ values.

blocks.caption: After sorting, a duplicate must sit right next to its twin.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n)** for the copy — or **O(1)** extra if you may sort `nums` itself.
3. A hash set of values seen

blocks.code:
def contains_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:                     # seen before: a duplicate
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** The fastest, at the price of a set as big as the input.

blocks.alt: Compare every pair: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Sort, then neighbours: O(n log n) time, O(1) in place space. Hash set: O(n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: Mention both 2 and 3: the set is faster, sorting saves memory. Interviewers like hearing the trade-off.

items: **The duplicates far apart** — `[1, 2, 3, 1]`; sorting brings them together.
**Negative numbers** — fine for both, but in JavaScript remember the numeric comparator.
**Sorting the caller's array** — `nums.sort()` changes their data; copy first if that matters.
**Contains Duplicate II** — a duplicate within k positions: a sliding window of a set.
**Contains Duplicate III** — values within t of each other within k positions: buckets of width t + 1.
**Minimum Absolute Difference** — the same sort-then-neighbours idea, looking for the closest pair. Next lesson.
